messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 43
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Physical Therapist
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 77

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Event Recall: Talking about the event, Trauma-Related Events: Trauma-related events
  Maladaptive Strategies: Compulsive Spending: I spend money impulsively to distract or comfort myself, Stay Near Exit: make sure to stay close to exit, Drug Use: take drugs
  Threat: Noticing Weapons: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
  Memory: More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things, No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself, Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
  Negative Appraisals: Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it, Unrecognisable Self: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me, Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened

Vignette:
Marama Tuilagi is a 43-year-old Fijian-American woman who has worked as a physical therapist for nearly fifteen years, a career she chose, as she once explained to her intake clinician, because she wanted to spend her professional life helping people recover. That conviction has become one of the more painful ironies of her current situation. Marama presents with a PCL-5 score of 77 and is seeking treatment approximately fourteen months after the event that she describes, with visible difficulty, as the worst night of her life.

It was a Saturday evening when Marama, after a long week of back-to-back patient appointments at the outpatient rehabilitation clinic where she works, attended a colleague's birthday gathering. She had been drinking — more than she intended — when she offered to drive a friend home, insisting she was fine. She was not fine. On a residential street less than two miles from the venue, she ran a stop sign and struck a cyclist. The man, a father in his late thirties, sustained a severe traumatic brain injury and spent weeks in intensive care. He survived, but with lasting neurological deficits. Marama was not charged criminally, but that fact has offered her no relief. In the weeks that followed, she told almost no one what had happened. She stopped attending social events. She stopped returning calls from the colleague whose party it had been. She has come to believe, with a certainty that feels immovable, that she will never forgive herself for not simply calling a cab, for not listening to the small voice that told her to wait, for not doing more to stop what was already in motion.

The smell of alcohol — at a restaurant, on a patient's breath, even from hand sanitiser with a particular ethanol sharpness — produces an immediate and visceral shift in Marama's state. In those moments the night returns not as a recollection but as something happening now: the jolt, the sound, the stillness that followed. These intrusions arrive with a vividness she describes as more real than anything she can ordinarily remember, and yet when she tries to construct a coherent account of the sequence of events, even privately and to herself, the narrative fractures. She cannot hold the whole story in order. What she is left with instead is shame — a wave of it that arrives reliably whenever the memory surfaces, a shame so total that she has come to feel she cannot think about the event at all without it overwhelming her completely.

At work, Marama moves through the rehabilitation gym with a vigilance that has become habitual. She scans the room — the resistance bands looped on hooks, the weighted bars, the parallel rails — registering each object with a quiet, automatic assessment she cannot fully explain but cannot stop. She positions herself near the door during group sessions, a habit that has not gone unnoticed by her supervisor, who has gently asked whether she is feeling well. Marama has deflected each time. Outside the clinic, she has spent money she cannot account for — online purchases arriving at her apartment in a steady stream, items she barely registers before they accumulate in corners — and she has, on a small number of occasions she disclosed with evident shame, used prescription medication obtained from sources she did not specify to get through particularly bad nights.

What has finally brought her to seek help is not any single event but an accumulation. Her partner of four years, a patient and steady man named David, told her recently and quietly that he did not recognise her anymore. The words landed because she had been thinking the same thing. The woman who had spent her career restoring function and movement in others now feels, in her own words, like a stranger inhabiting her own history. She is afraid, above all, that treatment will require her to speak about what happened — that talking about the event will confirm what she already suspects, that she will not be able to handle it. What she hopes for, tentatively and with no great confidence, is that some version of herself from before that Saturday night might still be recoverable.
